name: Corneal Dystrophy

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Genetic Diagnostic Criteria for Corneal Dystrophies

criteria.description: Presence of bilateral, progressive corneal opacities affecting specific corneal layers
Positive family history consistent with autosomal dominant or recessive inheritance
Identification of pathogenic variants in known corneal dystrophy-associated genes (e.g., TGFBI, CHST6)
Corneal biopsy showing characteristic deposits or changes in corneal layers

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Bilateral characteristic corneal opacities with either positive family history or genetic confirmation
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Genetic testing supports diagnosis but is not mandatory; clinical presentation and family history remain key.

pathognomonic.notes: Common in epithelial basement membrane dystrophy and other subtypes

common.symptomName: Decreased visual acuity due to corneal clouding
searchTerms: reduced sight due to corneal clouding

common.notes: Light sensitivity due to corneal irregularities

common.symptomName: Foreign body sensation in the eye

occasional.notes: May occur secondary to chronic erosions
Resulting from recurrent erosions or advanced dystrophy

searchTerms: sharp eye discomfort on surface injury

rare.notes: Secondary to severe erosions or infection
Due to angle involvement or scarring

laboratory: Corneal biopsy histopathology showing characteristic deposits (e.g., amyloid, hyaline)
Corneal epithelial cell irregularities on impression cytology
imaging: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy revealing corneal opacities and erosions
Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (OCT) showing corneal layer involvement
Confocal microscopy demonstrating abnormal corneal deposits
genetic: Mutations in TGFBI gene (e.g., R124H, R555W) associated with epithelial-stromal dystrophies
Mutations in CHST6 gene in macular corneal dystrophy
Other gene mutations depending on subtype (e.g., KRT3, KRT12)
other: Family history consistent with autosomal dominant or recessive inheritance
Clinical response to lubricants and therapeutic contact lenses

distinguishingFeatures: Progressive corneal thinning and ectasia rather than opacities
Secondary corneal edema due to endothelial dysfunction
History of intraocular surgery or trauma
Presence of corneal bullae rather than stromal deposits
Acute onset with pain, redness, discharge

redFlags: Severe ocular pain unresponsive to treatment
Signs of corneal infection or ulceration
references: Krachmer JH, Mannis MJ, Holland EJ. Cornea: Fundamentals, Diagnosis and Management. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2011.
Weiss JS, Møller HU, Aldave AJ, et al. IC3D Classification of Corneal Dystrophies—Edition 2. Cornea. 2015;34(2):117-159.
